title: Free fall and projectile motion
blurb: Calculate the speed and distance of a falling object, explain why mass does not matter, and split a projectile into its horizontal and vertical motions.
question: A pill bottle slides off a 1.25 m counter at 1.0 m/s just as its cap drops straight down from the same edge. Using g = 10 m/s², which lands first, and how far from the counter does the bottle land?

teach.body: Formally, free fall is motion under the influence of gravity alone, with air resistance ignored. In plain English: let go of anything and, if air does not get in the way, it speeds up downward by about 9.8 m/s every second. That rate is g, the free-fall acceleration (9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface; items may say 'use g = 10 m/s²'). A heavy object and a light one fall with the same g, so dropped together they land together.

head: Time (s)
Speed v = gt
Distance d = ½gt²
teach.caption: Speed grows in step with time; distance grows with time SQUARED. With g = 9.8 the 3 s values are 29.4 m/s and 44.1 m, which is why every stem states g.

teach.h: Two equations for a dropped object
teach.body: From rest: v = gt and d = ½gt². Thrown straight up, an object slows by g each second until it stops at the top, then falls back. At the top the velocity is zero for an instant, but the acceleration is still g downward: gravity never switches off. With g = 10 m/s², a ball launched up at 20 m/s takes 2 s to reach the top and 2 s to come back.

teach.h: A ball thrown straight up at 20 m/s
teach.caption: One straight line with slope −10 m/s² the whole way, including at t = 2 s, where v = 0. Zero velocity is not zero acceleration.

teach.h: A projectile is two motions at once
teach.caption: The two motions are independent. A ball thrown sideways and a ball dropped from the same height land at the same time. On level ground with no air, a 45° launch gives the longest range.

items: A ball rolls off a table 0.80 m high at 3.0 m/s. Use g = 10 m/s².
Time to fall (vertical only): 0.80 = ½ × 10 × t², so t² = 0.16 and t = 0.40 s.
Horizontal distance: constant 3.0 m/s × 0.40 s = 1.2 m.
Check: a ball simply dropped from the table also takes 0.40 s.

teach.caption: In real air, a falling object speeds up until drag balances its weight. It keeps falling, at a constant speed.

teach.body: Kendra, a pharmacy technician applying to a nursing program, knocks a pill bottle off a 1.25 m counter at 1.0 m/s just as the cap drops straight down from the same edge (g = 10 m/s²). Vertically both start at rest: 1.25 = ½ × 10 × t², t² = 0.25, t = 0.50 s, so they land together. The bottle keeps its 1.0 m/s sideways and lands 1.0 × 0.50 = 0.50 m from the counter.

teach.text: Heavier objects do not fall faster in free fall. At the top of a throw the acceleration is g, not zero. A projectile's horizontal velocity does not shrink (no air). A ball thrown sideways does not land later than one dropped. In d = ½gt², square t and keep the ½.

items: Free fall: gravity only, acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² down, the same for every mass.
From rest: v = gt, d = ½gt². Use the g the stem gives.
Top of a vertical throw: v = 0, a = g downward.
Projectile: horizontal velocity constant, vertical motion is free fall; time in the air comes from the height.
Terminal velocity: drag equals weight, so the acceleration is zero.

summary: You can now calculate the speed and distance of a dropped object, explain why mass does not change free-fall acceleration and describe the motion at the top of a throw. You can also split a projectile into constant horizontal motion and free-fall vertical motion and explain terminal velocity.

A.q: With no air present, a feather and a hammer are released together from the same height. Which reaches the ground first?
A.why: With no air resistance every object falls with the same acceleration g, so they land at the same time.

whyNot.0: A heavier object does not fall faster when air resistance is absent.
whyNot.1: The feather is slowed by air on Earth, but here there is no air.
whyNot.3: Shape matters through air resistance, and there is no air here.

A.q: A coin is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how fast is it moving after 1.5 s?

whyNot.0: About 11 m is the distance fallen (½ × 10 × 1.5²), not the speed.
whyNot.2: Divides g by t (10 ÷ 1.5) instead of multiplying.
whyNot.3: Squares the time (10 × 1.5²); speed grows linearly with time.

A.q: In projectile motion with air resistance ignored, which quantity stays constant during the flight?
A.why: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity stays constant. Gravity changes only the vertical velocity.

whyNot.0: Gravity changes the vertical velocity by g every second.
whyNot.1: The height changes as the projectile rises and falls.
whyNot.2: Total speed changes because the vertical part changes.

B.q: A ball is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how far does it fall in 3.0 s? (d = ½gt²)

whyNot.3: 30 m/s is the speed after 3.0 s, not the distance.

B.q: A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how long does it take to reach its highest point?
B.why: The ball loses 10 m/s each second: 20 ÷ 10 = 2.0 s until its velocity reaches zero at the top.

whyNot.1: Multiplies speed by g instead of dividing.
whyNot.3: 4.0 s is the round trip, up and back down.

B.q: Why does a falling skydiver eventually stop speeding up?
options: Air drag grows until it equals her weight
Air drag becomes larger than her weight
Her mass falls as she gains speed
B.why: Drag rises with speed. When it equals her weight, the net force is zero, so her acceleration is zero: terminal velocity.

whyNot.0: Gravity barely changes over a skydive; the change is in air drag.
whyNot.2: Drag larger than weight would slow her down, not hold her speed steady.
whyNot.3: Mass does not change with speed in everyday physics.

C.q: A ball rolls off a table 0.45 m high at 4.0 m/s. Using g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, how far from the table does it land? (d = ½gt²)
C.why: 0.45 = ½ × 10 × t², so t² = 0.09 and t = 0.30 s. Horizontal distance = 4.0 × 0.30 = 1.2 m.

whyNot.0: Multiplies speed by height (4.0 × 0.45); the distance needs the fall time.
whyNot.1: Uses t² (0.09) as if it were t: 4.0 × 0.09 = 0.36.
whyNot.2: Assumes a 1.0 s fall instead of solving for the time.

C.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 6.0 m/s from a cliff and lands 2.0 s later. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², what is its horizontal velocity just before it lands?
C.why: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity stays at its launch value, 6.0 m/s.

whyNot.0: 20 m/s is the vertical velocity after 2.0 s (10 × 2.0), not the horizontal one.
whyNot.2: Adds the vertical and horizontal speeds; they are separate components.
whyNot.3: Halves the launch speed as if something slowed it; with no air, no horizontal force acts.

C.q: A stone is dropped from rest and falls freely for 2.0 s. Using g = 9.8 m/s², how far does it fall? (d = ½gt²)

reteach.title: The ball dropped on a moving train
reteach.question: A passenger on a smooth, steadily moving train drops a ball. Why does it land at her feet and not behind her?

blocks.h: It keeps the train's sideways speed
blocks.body: Before she lets go, the ball moves forward with the train. After release, nothing pushes it backward (ignore air), so it keeps that forward speed while gravity pulls it down. To her it falls straight down. To someone on the platform it traces a curve: constant forward speed plus free fall. That curve is projectile motion, and the fall takes exactly as long as a drop in a stationary room.

blocks.text: Sideways speed changes where a projectile lands, never how long it takes to fall. The height alone sets the time.

explain.body: From rest the speed grows by g every second: v = gt. Mass does not appear in the formula.

explain.caption: Speed after each second with g = 10 m/s².

test.q: A pebble is dropped down a well and falls freely for 2.5 s. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², what is its speed at that moment?

whyNot.0: About 31 m is the distance fallen (½ × 10 × 2.5²), not the speed.
whyNot.3: Squares the time (10 × 2.5²); speed is linear in t.

explain.body: Rising, the object slows by g each second; at the top v = 0; falling, it speeds up by g each second. The acceleration is g downward at every point.

test.q: A volleyball is tossed straight up. Ignoring air resistance, which statement is true at its highest point?
options: Velocity and acceleration both point up
Gravity stops acting for an instant
Its velocity is zero; it still accelerates
test.why: At the top the ball stops for an instant (v = 0), but gravity still gives it an acceleration of g downward.

whyNot.0: Zero velocity is not zero acceleration; gravity keeps acting.
whyNot.1: At the top the velocity is zero, and the acceleration points down.

explain.body: Sideways speed and vertical fall do not affect each other. The fall time depends on the height and g alone.

test.q: A marble rolls off a table at 2.0 m/s just as an identical marble is dropped from the same height. Ignoring air resistance, which reaches the floor first?
options: They land at the same time
It depends on the rolling speed
test.why: Both start with zero vertical velocity and fall with g from the same height, so they take the same time.

whyNot.1: Rolling speed carries the marble farther, not down faster.
whyNot.2: The dropped marble does not fall faster; its vertical motion is identical.
whyNot.3: The fall time depends on height and g, not on horizontal speed.

explain.body: With air, drag grows with speed. When drag equals weight the net force is zero, so the object falls at a constant speed.

test.q: A skydiver is falling at terminal velocity. What is her acceleration?
test.why: At terminal velocity drag equals weight, so the net force and the acceleration are both zero.

whyNot.0: That is her acceleration at the start, before drag builds up.
whyNot.2: An upward acceleration would slow her; at terminal velocity her speed is steady.
whyNot.3: Her speed has stopped rising, so the acceleration is not increasing.
